title: Easter is fifty days
hook: Christ is risen! He is risen indeed! Orthodox Pascha often falls on a later date, by the old calendar

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holy Saturday, and your line: light in the dark. This week walked the hardest road: ashes, Lent, palms, a towel, a cross, a silent tomb. Seventeen weeks on the path. Today, the stone moves. Day one hundred nineteen.

Midnight, outside an Orthodox church. Hundreds of people holding candles in the street, some of them kids who are way past bedtime. The priest steps out and shouts, in Greek, Christ is risen! And the whole crowd shouts back: Truly he is risen! He says it again, and again, louder. Then there are fireworks, bells, and people kissing each other three times on the cheek. For weeks afterward, friends greet each other that way on the street and even in text messages. In English-speaking churches you'll hear it as: Christ is risen! He is risen indeed! It all goes back to a Sunday morning, and some women at an empty tomb, where an angel says, "He is not here: for he is risen, as he said." Today's word is the oldest name for the feast.
screen: `MIDNIGHT, CANDLES IN THE STREET.` → `CHRIST IS RISEN!` → `HE IS NOT HERE.`

segments.voice: Pascha. It's the Greek and Latin name for Easter, and it comes from the Hebrew Pesach, Passover. Jesus died and rose at Passover time, and the first Christians, who were Jewish, heard his death and rising as a new passing over, from death to life. That's why, in most of the world's languages, Easter is some form of Pascha: Pâques in French, Pascua in Spanish. English is unusual with Easter, a word whose origin is still debated. The greeting comes from Luke. When two disciples rush back to Jerusalem, the others meet them with the news: "The Lord is risen indeed." Now, the date. Easter falls on the first Sunday after the first full moon of spring. But Orthodox churches still count by the older Julian calendar, so Orthodox Pascha often falls later, by a week or even five, and some years both land on the same day. Families with a foot in both traditions sometimes celebrate twice. And here's the part many people miss: Easter isn't a day either. Like Christmas, it's a season, and a longer one. Fifty days, all the way to Pentecost. Churches keep the candles burning and the alleluias going. For Christians, this is the center of everything. Paul put it bluntly: "And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain." Christians say that's exactly why they keep shouting it back, for fifty days: he is risen indeed.
screen: `PASCHA, FROM PESACH: PASSOVER.` · `THE LORD IS RISEN INDEED.` · `THE FULL MOON AND TWO CALENDARS.` · `FIFTY DAYS, NOT ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry good news. Settle, and breathe. Think of the women running from the tomb, scared and overjoyed at the same time, with news they could barely say. Now think of one piece of good news in your own life, or someone else's, that deserves to be told. A recovery. A new job. A kindness someone doesn't know about. Picture the person who should hear it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it first. If you don't, just let yourself feel how good it is. Then plan to tell them today. The bell holds the time.
Pascha. The Greek and Latin name for Easter, from the Hebrew for Passover. A feast of fifty days. Today's word.
Your line: he is risen indeed. Today, greet someone with good news, the way the first ones ran with theirs. Day one hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Christians celebrate Easter, or Pascha, with services at dawn, at the vigil or at midnight, greeting one another with Christ is risen and the reply He is risen indeed; many churches keep the Easter season for fifty days, to Pentecost.

fork.setup: you're one of the women at the tomb. the stone is rolled away, and an angel says he is not here, for he is risen. what do you do?
options: stay at the tomb to be sure.
run to tell the disciples, afraid and overjoyed.
go home and tell no one.
fork.reveal: in Matthew they leave "with fear and great joy" and run to tell. Mark's ending says they were afraid and said nothing, at least at first.

original.note: Greek: Passover, and the name for Easter, from Hebrew Pesach.

trapdoor: what you thought: an Orthodox word for Easter.
what it means: the feast of the resurrection, named for Passover, kept for fifty days, with the greeting he is risen indeed.
what a scholar hears: Greek pascha from Aramaic and Hebrew Pesach; since the Council of Nicaea churches aimed to keep one Sunday, but the Julian and Gregorian calendars now split the date.

notes: Date rule simplified to 'the first Sunday after the first full moon of spring' (ecclesiastical full moon on or after March 21). Orthodox Pascha can be the same day or one, four or five weeks later. Confirm.
Greek greeting 'Christos anesti / Alithos anesti' rendered as 'Christ is risen! Truly he is risen!'. Confirm.
English 'Easter' origin (Bede's Eostre and alternatives) left as 'still debated'. Confirm.
Luke 24:34: the eleven greet the two from Emmaus with 'The Lord is risen indeed'. Confirm the summary.
Mark 16:8 (short ending: they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid) mentioned in the fork reveal with 'at least at first'; confirm wording.
